 Federal tech fellows would get an expedited path to permanent jobs under a new bill 
 While the Trump administration’s Tech Force initiative assigns young tech employees to agencies for two-year tours, the sponsor of a new House measure wants to “open the door” to longer-term service. 
 Sean Michael Newhouse 
 | 
 November 16, 2026 03:57 PM ET
 Congress
 Early Career
 Civil Service 
 Sean Michael Newhouse 
 Staff Reporter 
 As the government struggles to recruit tech talent, a House Democrat recently introduced legislation that aims to make it easier for agencies to convert short-term science- and technology-focused employees into career federal workers. 
 Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Va., a co-chair of the Federal Workforce Caucus, argued his bill is necessary because of agency fellowships such as Tech Force , a Trump administration initiative that places early-career technologists in government roles for two-year stints. 
 “These professionals are writing code that delivers services to Americans, securing networks that keep our data safe and supporting research that saves lives,” he said in a statement . “If they want to keep serving, we should open the door to a long-term career in federal service.”
 Under the Keep Federal Tech Talent Act ( H.R. 10960 ), agencies would be authorized to convert qualified employees serving in time-limited positions focused on STEM, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and data science, into career competitive service appointments. Agencies also could provide student loan repayments and professional development benefits as incentives to such workers and would be required to annually report how often they use this authority. 
 Walkinshaw’s bill is endorsed by the National Federation of Federal Employees and the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers. 
 “At a time when the federal workforce has just endured a massive loss of personnel and expertise in STEM and highly skilled roles , we look to Congress to find urgent solutions that strengthen the federal talent pipeline,” said IFPTE President Matt Biggs in a statement. “That’s why IFPTE supports the Keep Federal Tech Talent Act, legislation that seeks to ensure that temporary federal employees are given opportunities to continue their careers in the civil service.” 
 Scott Kupor — the director of the Office of Personnel Management, which is managing Tech Force — has pitched the program and other early-career hiring initiatives by arguing that a person who completes a couple years of government service would develop a skill set that is valuable in the private sector. 
 But Arun Gupta — the CEO of the NobleReach Foundation, a nonprofit that is a partner of Tech Force — also contended at a government tech panel during the National Academy of Public Administration’s conference last week that temporary placement programs like Tech Force are ideal methods for agencies to recruit permanent employees. 
 “What you find is that if the hiring manager likes the person, and the employee likes the job, they'll figure out a way to convert them [to career],” he said. “Actually, that’s probably the way this should work. Why are we giving full-time employment to someone that hasn't even been there before?” 
 In his press release announcing the measure, Walkinshaw connected it to his push for a 2027 pay raise for federal employees .
 “A pay freeze is a pay cut, and it’s one more barrier to attracting top talent,” he said. “We can’t ask these professionals to consider a career in government and then tell them their work isn’t worth fair pay.”
